hints: Look at how the carbon skeleton changes, the product has one more carbon than the starting bromoalkane, so focus on how that extra carbon is added.
The first step replaces Br with CN by nucleophilic substitution, so think about which reagent is the best source of free cyanide ions.
The second step converts a nitrile into a free -COOH group, so consider whether you need acidic or alkaline conditions to finish with the acid itself.
walkthrough:
**Spot the chain extension**

Well done for noticing the carbon count. 1-bromopropane has 3 carbons and butanenitrile and butanoic acid both have 4 carbons.

This tells you the CN group provides the extra carbon: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$$

**Choose X for Br to CN**

This is nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane. You need a good supply of $\text{CN}^-$ ions to replace $\text{Br}^-$.

The standard reagent is potassium cyanide in ethanol: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + \text{Br}^-$$

**Choose Y for nitrile to acid**

Nitriles can be hydrolysed by heating with aqueous acid to give the carboxylic acid directly. Heating with aqueous alkali would stop at the carboxylate salt, $\text{RCOO}^-$.

So you need dilute $\text{HCl(aq)}$ with heat: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_4^+$$

**Combine to select the pair**

X must be $\text{KCN}$ in $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ and Y must be $\text{HCl(aq)}$. That combination gives the nitrile intermediate and then the free carboxylic acid.

options.A: NH3 would do nucleophilic substitution to give a primary amine, CH3CH2CH2NH2, not a nitrile. It does not add a carbon, so you could never reach the 4-carbon acid.
options.B: X is correct here, but Y is wrong. Heating a nitrile with NaOH(aq) gives alkaline hydrolysis to the carboxylate ion, CH3CH2CH2COO-, not the free butanoic acid. You would need a second acidification step.
options.C: Exactly right. KCN in C2H5OH supplies CN- for substitution to form butanenitrile, then HCl(aq) with heat gives acid hydrolysis of the nitrile to free butanoic acid.
options.D: HCN is a weak acid and is mainly used with a trace of NaCN for addition to aldehydes and ketones, not for substitution of a bromoalkane. You need ionic KCN for a good yield of the nitrile, and NaOH(aq) alone would give the salt, not the acid.
